# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum stood between a locksmith and a bakery, in a building so narrow that visitors sometimes walked past it sideways without noticing. Its sign had been painted by someone who got as far as THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED and then apparently remembered an appointment. For thirty-one years, nobody had added the final word. Rain had softened the lettering. Pigeons nested behind the M. On sunny mornings, the baker propped open his door, and the whole first gallery smelled of bread.

Lena arrived on a Tuesday carrying a cardboard box and wearing the expression of someone who had rehearsed a practical question to avoid asking an emotional one.

“Do you accept donations?” she asked.

The man behind the desk was repairing a pencil sharpener. Small brass pieces lay on a cloth before him. He wore a green cardigan with three different buttons.

“Sometimes,” he said. “What have you brought?”

“A ship.”

He looked at the box.

“A modest ship,” she added.

Inside, wrapped in a tea towel, lay a wooden model of a three-masted schooner. Its hull was painted blue. Two masts stood upright; the third rested loose along the deck. Threads hung from the rigging like the roots of a plant pulled out too soon. There were six tiny cannons, a coil of rope, and a captain no taller than a fingernail, still attached to the plastic frame in which he had been manufactured.

“My father made it,” Lena said. Then, because accuracy had become important since his death: “He made most of it.”

The man did not touch the ship.

“Was he planning to finish?”

“For twenty years.”

“That isn’t quite what I asked.”

Lena looked toward the door. Across the street, a woman was persuading a reluctant dog to pass a drainpipe.

“I think he liked planning to finish.”

The man smiled, not triumphantly, but as if she had supplied an essential measurement.

“That,” he said, “is something we understand here.”

His name was Ansel. He gave her a donation form on which the usual questions—name, address, description—were followed by several unusual ones.

*Was the object abandoned, interrupted, or released?*

*Does anyone still expect it to become something else?*

*Would its maker be relieved to know where it is?*

Lena tapped the second question with the pen.

“How could I possibly know?”

“You may write that.”

She did. In the next blank, after thinking for a while, she wrote it again.

While Ansel made tea, she wandered into the museum. The first room contained a sweater with one sleeve, a chessboard on which a game had stopped after eleven moves, and a stack of pages titled *A Brief History of Everything Important*. The stack was not especially large. Beside it stood a violin whose maker had carved the body but never attached the neck. The wood had darkened to the color of honey held against a window.

Every object had a label. None included a monetary value.

*Wedding speech, never delivered. The speaker decided, correctly, that the joke would hurt his brother.*

*Garden plan, abandoned after the discovery that the supposedly dead pear tree was alive.*

*First chapter of a detective novel. Donated by the author upon beginning a different detective novel.*

Lena stopped before a pair of small red mittens joined by a long string. One mitten lacked a thumb. Its label read simply: *No further information requested.*

In the second room, a woman was sitting beside a half-completed jigsaw puzzle of the sea. All the edge pieces were in place. The center was a scattering of blue.

“Are visitors allowed to work on things?” Lena asked.

“No,” the woman said.

“Then what are you doing?”

“Looking.”

“Sorry.”

“People always ask.”

The woman studied a piece near her elbow, turned it once, and put it down without trying to fit it anywhere. Lena found this unexpectedly irritating.

Ansel brought the tea in two cups that did not match.

“Why preserve any of it?” she asked him. “There must be millions of unfinished things.”

“There are millions of finished things. People preserve those.”

“Yes, but they’re—”

She stopped.

“Better?” he suggested.

“Easier to explain.”

“That’s true.”

He sat on a bench beneath a map of an imaginary country. The western coast was elaborately inked; the east dissolved into pencil marks and a note that said *mountains, perhaps*. Lena noticed that somebody had drawn a railway to the uncertain mountains.

Her father had kept the ship on a table in the spare room. Every winter he announced that this would be the winter. He bought glue, finer brushes, a magnifying lamp. He subscribed to a magazine about model boats, although he had no interest in actual sailing and disliked water deeper than his knees. When Lena visited, she would ask about his progress. He always said, “Getting there.” In later years, she had begun answering, “Where, exactly?”

Now she wished she hadn’t. Not because he had seemed hurt—he had usually laughed—but because the joke had hardened into her account of him. Her father, who could never finish anything. Her father, with his loose cupboard handles and stacks of unread books. She had repeated it so often that she had forgotten he worked for forty years in a hospital laundry, where everything had to be finished by six.

“I don’t want it in my flat,” she said.

“All right.”

“But I don’t want to throw it away.”

“All right.”

“And I don’t want you to pretend it’s a masterpiece.”

Ansel glanced into the box.

“The second mast is noticeably crooked.”

Lena laughed. She had not expected to, and it came out roughly.

“We can keep it,” he said. “But not as evidence against him.”

She looked up.

“Objects are sometimes donated in that spirit. We try to discourage it.”

She returned the following Saturday. She told herself she wanted to see where they had put the ship, but it was still in the little office behind the desk, waiting for a stand. Ansel was on the telephone, saying, “No, an unpaid electricity bill is unfinished in a different sense.”

When he hung up, he asked if she could hold two pieces of wood together while he measured them.

“I’m not volunteering,” she said.

“Of course not.”

She held them for twenty minutes.

By the end of the month, she had a key.

The work was less romantic than she had imagined. There were floors to sweep, emails to answer, and a damp patch in the ceiling that looked increasingly like an accusation. Ansel kept the accounts in a ledger whose columns never quite agreed. Lena, who managed invoices for a wholesaler, found this intolerable. She made a spreadsheet. He regarded it with polite suspicion until it revealed that the museum had been paying for two telephone lines, one of which ended in a cupboard.

Donations came in irregularly. A retired bus driver brought a papier-mâché moon. A student offered thirty-seven seconds of an animated film in which a fox opened a door. A man carried in a stone he had intended to sculpt into his wife’s likeness.

“Does she know?” Lena asked.

“She told me to get it out of the garage.”

They accepted the moon and the fox. The stone, after discussion, went into the little courtyard, where it became a place to sit.

Not everything belonged. Ansel refused a collection of letters someone had stolen from an ex-lover.

“But they’re unfinished,” the man protested.

“They’re also hers.”

A woman wanted to donate her daughter’s sketchbooks because the daughter had decided to become an electrician.

“Ask her first,” Lena said.

“She doesn’t care about them.”

“Then asking should be easy.”

The woman left offended and returned two weeks later with her daughter, who donated one sketchbook and took the rest home.

In April, Ansel fell on the bakery steps and broke his ankle. From his hospital bed, he gave Lena elaborate instructions about feeding the courtyard birds, though none about the museum itself.

“Shouldn’t we close until you’re back?”

“Would you like to?”

She thought about her evenings, which had become crowded with dusting and label writing. She thought about the ship, now resting on its stand between a half-woven basket and an unfinished translation of a poem.

“No,” she said.

“Then don’t.”

Without him, visitors asked her questions she could not answer. Why had the violin maker stopped? Had the red mittens belonged to a child who died? Was the chess game interrupted by war?

Sometimes the records supplied ordinary explanations. The violin maker developed an allergy to the varnish. The chess players got hungry, and one knocked the board over while reaching for his coat. Sometimes there was no explanation at all.

“Surely you could find out,” a visitor said.

Lena looked at the mittens.

“Possibly,” she replied.

The first school group arrived in May. Twenty-three children entered with the collective momentum of a dropped tray. Their teacher apologized before anybody had done anything.

Lena had prepared a talk about creativity and perseverance. Three sentences into it, a boy pointed at the sweater and asked, “Why didn’t they just make the other sleeve?”

“We don’t know.”

“Maybe they only had one arm,” another child said.

“Maybe,” Lena replied.

The teacher began to correct them, then thought better of it.

They spent half an hour inventing explanations for the exhibits. The imaginary country had lost funding. The fox behind the animated door was waiting for a parcel. The ship’s captain refused to sail until someone released him from his plastic frame.

At the end, a quiet girl stayed beside the jigsaw puzzle.

“My mum says I have to finish every book I start,” she said.

“What does your teacher say?”

The teacher, collecting coats nearby, suddenly became very interested in a zip.

In June, a letter arrived from the building’s owner. He intended to sell. The museum could purchase the premises at a price so far beyond its means that Lena initially assumed a decimal point had been omitted.

Ansel read the letter twice.

“Well,” he said.

“That’s it?”

“I’m waiting to see if another word helps.”

She paced the office. They could apply for grants, start a fundraiser, contact newspapers. There must be foundations interested in overlooked cultural institutions.

“There are,” Ansel said. “They receive many applications.”

“So we write a good one.”

They spent three weeks on the application. Lena described the collection as an archive of interrupted creative practice. Ansel crossed out “interrupted” and wrote “unfinished.” She restored “interrupted” because the foundation’s guidelines used it.

They counted visitors. They photographed the galleries. They attached testimonials, a budget, and a plan for expanding educational outreach.

Under *Demonstrated outcomes*, Lena wrote three sentences, deleted them, and went to look at the ship.

The loose threads had gathered dust. Carefully, she cleaned them with a soft brush.

The foundation declined. So did another. A local newspaper ran a cheerful article under the headline MUSEUM MAY NEVER BE FINISHED, which produced forty-six visitors, twelve donations, and enough money to pay the electricity bill.

Lena began staying late. She made lists at home. She woke thinking of people she might contact.

One evening, she found Ansel removing labels from an empty display case.

“What are you doing?”

“Planning.”

“For closing?”

“For what happens next.”

She felt a sharp, unreasonable anger.

“You could try harder.”

He set down the label.

“Yes,” he said. “I could.”

The simplicity of his answer stopped her.

“I’ve been here thirty-one years, Lena. I wanted somewhere these things could be kept without apology. For thirty-one years, there has been somewhere. I’m not sure losing the building makes all of that a failure.”

She wanted to argue. Instead, she sat beside him.

Beyond the wall, the baker was dragging racks across his floor. The locksmith’s bell rang. Someone outside laughed so loudly that they both turned toward the sound.

“What will happen to everything?” she asked.

“We’ll ask.”

And they did. They wrote to donors and their families. Some wanted their objects back; others did not. A library offered space for the imaginary map and several manuscripts. The local school adopted the papier-mâché moon. The animated fox went online, where viewers supplied hundreds of theories about what stood behind the door. The woman who watched the jigsaw puzzle took it home.

“Will you finish it?” Lena asked.

“Perhaps. I’ve retired.”

The answer pleased her more than she expected.

On the final Saturday, the museum was crowded. People moved slowly through rooms that had seemed too small when full and now looked smaller as they emptied. The baker brought rolls. The locksmith fixed the office latch without being asked.

Lena packed her father’s ship. Beneath its stand she found Ansel’s label, which she had somehow never read closely.

*Model schooner, worked on intermittently over twenty years. According to the donor, its maker enjoyed having it to look forward to.*

She wrapped the loose mast separately.

At home, she put the ship on a low shelf near the window. It occupied the space where she had intended to keep a houseplant, once she found a kind she could reliably keep alive. In daylight, the blue paint revealed small variations: darker beneath the rail, thin near the stern. One cannon pointed inward. Her father must have noticed. Perhaps he had meant to fix it. Perhaps he had decided nobody would come aboard from that direction.

A week later, Lena bought a small pair of cutters. She sat at her kitchen table, lifted the plastic frame from the box, and carefully freed the captain. Then she placed him on the deck. He leaned slightly, but stayed upright. She carried the ship back to the shelf, washed the tea towel, and put it in the drawer with her others.
